name: The Law of Multiple Proportions
statement: When two elements form several compounds, the mass ratios are small whole numbers.
meaning: When two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other stand in ratios of small whole numbers. Fix the amount of carbon and the oxygen in carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide falls in a ratio of one to two. The pattern is a direct fingerprint of atoms combining in whole-number counts.
mechanism: Because compounds are made of whole atoms combined in whole-number ratios, the mass of one element per fixed mass of the other must jump in discrete, small-integer steps from one compound to the next. There is no way to combine half an atom, so the masses cannot vary continuously; they move in clean multiples. This discreteness, showing up at the macroscopic scale of weighable masses, is precisely why the law was such powerful evidence for the existence of atoms.

examples.text: For a fixed mass of carbon, the oxygen in carbon monoxide and in carbon dioxide is in a ratio of one to two — the classic demonstration of the law.
Across the several oxides of nitrogen, the oxygen combined with a fixed mass of nitrogen runs through small whole-number ratios, the exact series depending on which oxides are compared.
For a fixed mass of hydrogen, hydrogen peroxide holds twice the oxygen of water, a one-to-two ratio between the two compounds of the same elements.

variants.name: The stoichiometric laws
variants.text: The trio with definite proportions and conservation of mass; multiple proportions concerns relationships between different compounds of the same elements, definite proportions the fixed composition of a single one.

variants.name: Evidence for atomism
variants.text: The piece of the stoichiometric evidence that most directly implied atoms, since whole-number mass steps are exactly what discrete combining particles would produce.

whyItMatters: It was, of the classical stoichiometric laws, the one that pointed most directly to the atom: small whole-number mass ratios are just what one expects if matter combines in discrete units. Formulated by Dalton as part of his atomic theory, it helped turn atomism from speculation into the organising principle of chemistry, even if its practical use is now largely historical.

working.lead: Compare compounds of the same pair
working.text: to see the law, hold one element's mass fixed and compare the other's mass across the different compounds the two form.
expect the resulting mass ratios to reduce to small whole numbers for simple compounds, the signature of whole-atom combination.

working.lead: Keep it distinct from definite proportions
working.text: remember it concerns relations between different compounds, not the fixed composition of any single one.

limits: The law is most striking for simple inorganic compounds with small formulas. For large molecules the ratios stop being usefully small — decane and undecane give a hydrogen-mass ratio of a hundred and twenty-one to a hundred and twenty, whole numbers but hardly small. Non-stoichiometric compounds, whose composition varies, violate it, and isotopes complicate the exact mass ratios, so deuterium-containing compounds do not cleanly obey it. Rounding errors distort computed ratios for the lightest elements. Historically vital as evidence for the atom, it is of limited modern practical use now that atomic structure is directly known.
misreadings: It must not be confused with the law of definite proportions — the commonest error. Definite proportions says one compound always has the same fixed composition; multiple proportions compares two or more different compounds of the same elements and finds small-integer mass ratios between them. And it does not apply universally: large molecules, non-stoichiometric compounds, and isotopic variation all strain or break it.
origin: Formulated by John Dalton around 1803-1804 as a central part of his atomic theory; named the doctrine of multiple proportions by Berzelius in 1813, its verification across many compounds gave crucial support to the existence of atoms.
